3. All the petitioners were included in the MPO list and they received the government portions of salary for years together. In the year 2006 the result of Degree Examination of those colleges were too poor for which the Government decided to stop the payment of salary of the petitioners though MPO and accordingly issued the impugned letter being No. শাঃ১৩/ফবি/৫-৩/২০০৬/৬৬০ dated 26-5-2008 (Annexure-A) without assigning any reason through which the petitioners have been deprived of from the MPOs from the said date. 

 4. The petitioners further asserted that all the examinees did not obtain zero marks in all the subjects, and actually some students have obtained pass marks in almost all subjects except in English for which the result of the said colleges become poor which is purely an accident which has happened not only for the examinees of the petitioner's colleges but also for the examinees of hundreds of other colleges, including Government colleges which was reported in different newspapers that English script of that examination was out of syllabus. The further cause of such failure of the students is the initiation of two years graduation course into three years course. The petitioner further asserted that not only Non-Government recognized colleges have such unsatisfactory result in Degree Pass examination of 2006, held in 2007, but the same have also happened in case of large number of Government Colleges which reveals from the National University published list, showing 68 colleges have the zero result in the Degree Pass Examination of 2006, out of which 15 colleges were Government Colleges namely: Tala Government College, Shaheed Bulbul College, Ulipur Government College, Kurigram, Begum Rokeya Government College, Rangpur, Thakurgaon Government College, Chandpur Government College, Sonagazi Government College, Senbagh Government College, Noakhali, Melandah Government College, Jamalpur, Narshingdhi Government College, Narshingdhi including some other Government Colleges. But the salary of the teachers of the said government colleges not having been stopped due to the same fault and, as such, the Government decision to stop the MPOs of the aforesaid 14 colleges is discriminatory in effete. 

 7. The learned Advocate Mr ABM Nurul Islam along with the learned Advocate Mr Md Giausuddin, appearing on behalf of the petitioners upon placing before us the writ petition and the annexures thereof submits that the Government by the impugned Memo No. শাঃ১১/বিবিধ-৫/৯৪ (অংশ-৬)/৩৯৫ dated 26-5-2008 stopped the salary payment of the petitioners though MPOs of the aforesaid colleges relying upon the "Paripatra" being No. ',Its/1r-Att-a.C4.8 dated 24th October, 1995 where as the said "Paripatra" has no force of law within the meaning of law as defined in Article 152 of the Constitution and thus the impugned order passed by the respondent Government is illegal and without any lawful authority. 

 8. The learned Senior Counsel Mr Nurul Islam, further submits that circular issued by the ministry of Education known as Janobal Kathamo, 1995" does not provide any such provision that for securing 'zero result', payment of salaries through MPOs of the teachers and staffs of the colleges concerned will be stopped for indefinite period despite which the government through the impugned letter cancelled the MPOs without assigning any reason which is illegal and must be treated as issued without lawful authority. 

 9. The learned senior counsel further argues that Article 15 of "Janabal Kathamo, 1995" does not authorize the respondent Government to cancel the MPOs of any Educational Institution as a whole on the ground of 'zero result' of the institution, but in the instant case the respondents stopped the MPOs of all the teachers and staffs of the aforesaid colleges without assigning any reason which is illegal and without any lawful authority. The learned senior counsel Mr ABM Nurul Islam contends that as many as 68 colleges secured zero result in the degree examination of the year 2006 held in 2007, whereas the respondent- Government cancelled the MPOs only for the petitioners 14 colleges which is illegal as well as discriminatory action of the respondent and therefore the same is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority. 

 10. The learned Senior Counsel Mr Islam further argues that it is a rule of law that once a benefit is given to any person the same cannot be curtailed without giving him an opportunity of being heard. But in the instant case the respondent-Government without making any enquiry or without obtaining any report from the concerned Education Board cancelled the MPOs of the aforesaid 14 colleges which is illegal and without lawful authority. 

 11. The learned senior counsel further submits that the result of the degree examination of 2006 held in 2007 was not satisfactory in general which has been proved from the result of 68 colleges including some Government colleges which secured zero result. 

 12. The learned Senior Counsel Mr ABM Nurul Islam finally argues that the Education is the backbone of our nation which requires utmost care of the Ministry of Education for the smooth functioning of the Educational Institutions but unfortunately the Government has been dealing with the educational affairs through 16 "Paripatra" i.e. circulars which were formulated to save the interest of some vested quarters for their illegal gain and thus a direction is required from this court directing the government to arrange for promulgation of an uniform law and Regulation for the sake of better educational atmosphere in the country. Thus he prayed for making the Rule absolute. 

 13. The learned Assistant Attorney General Mr Md Iqbal Hossain, appearing on behalf of the respondent-Government, on the other hand, submits that for the better functioning and improvement of the educational institutions of the country, the Government exercises a supervisory control over the Educational Institutions and provides the salary of the teachers and staffs of the educational institutions and, as such, the Government has power to stop the salary of the teachers and staffs of the colleges for a limited period. He argues that the question of discrimination does knot arise at all since the payments of salary and after benefits to the teachers and staffs of the Government colleges are guided by separate set of rules. 

 14. The learned Assistant Attorney General further argues that the educational institutions are being guided by the Provision of Act 33 of 1961 and the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education has been authorized to make the regulation for smooth functioning of the schools and Intermediate colleges, but no provision has been made in the said Act for the grant of MPOs Therefore the Government under the provision of the aforesaid "Paripatra" grants salary through the MPOs to the teachers and staffs of the colleges and for better improvement of the Educational Institution the government is authorized to stop the payment of salary for a limited period and if the result of the aforesaid colleges thereafter improves, then the Government may withdraw the stoppage of salary. The learned Assistant Attorney General prays for discharge of the Rule. 

 16. The petitioners are the teachers and staffs of 14 colleges who were receiving the government portion of their salary through the Monthly Payments Order (MPO) list. In the year 2006 the Degree students of those colleges, who have participated in the 2006 Degree examination could not pass and accordingly the pass rate of the Degree students of those colleges for the year 2006 became zero. Finding such results of those colleges in the Degree examination of 2006, the Government in the Ministry of Education became annoyed and the impugned order Annexure-A discloses that a show cause notice was served upon those 14 colleges to show cause as to why the government portion of the salary of the teachers and staffs of those 14 colleges shall not be cancelled. 

 17. Having received no reply upon such show cause notice from those 14 colleges, the government issued the impugned letter 'Annexure-A' directing the Director General, Intermediate and Higher Education Directorate to stop the MPOs of the petitioners and accordingly the same have been stopped. In order to pass the said order the government purportedly relied upon clause No. 15 of the বেসরকারী শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান (মহাবিদ্যালয় সমূহ) এর শিক্ষক কর্মচারীদের বেতন ভাতাদির সরকারি অংশ প্রদান এবং জনবল কাঠামো সম্পর্কিত নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫. 

 18. Now the pertinent question raised before this Court whether the government is empowered under the said clause No. 15 of the নীতিমালা, ১৯৯৫ to stop the MPO of the petitioners on the allegation that none of the students of those 14 colleges were passed in the Degree Examination of 2006. 

 19. Upon examination of the aforesaid নীতিমালা, ১৯৯৫ it appears that the government upon its governmental duty in the Ministry of Education made decisions to pay certain portion of the salary of the teachers and staffs of all the qualified educational institution of the country out of the government fund and in order to materialize the said decision upon sound principle formulated two Nitimalas separately for the secondary schools and the colleges of the country. The বেসরকারী শিক্ষা প্রতিষ্ঠান (মহাবিদ্যালয় সমূহ) এর শিক্ষক কর্মচারীদের বেতন ভাতাদির সরকারি অংশ প্রদান এবং জনবল কাঠামো সম্পর্কিত নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ hereinafter be mentioned as Nitimala 1995, is one of such Policy formulation applicable for the colleges under which government continued to pay the government portion of the salary to the teachers and staffs of the colleges. The petitioners being the teachers and staffs of those 14 colleges were listed in the MPO under the provision of the said Nitimala 1995 as they were found eligible to receive the same under it. Therefore this Court finds that the provision of the said Nitimala 1995 is applicable against the petitioners so far the MPO payments is concerned. 

 20. From the provision of the aforesaid clause 15, it appears that the government is empowered to cancel stop, curtail or temporarily stay the payment of MPO on certain grounds which does not include the failure of the students in passing the public examination. But upon perusal of clause 6 of the said নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ it appears that a precondition has been imposed in order to avail the MPO as to the pass rate of the students in the public examination. Clause 6 of the নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ is reproduced below: 

 21. It appears from the underlined provision that the provision of article 6 of the নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ is applicable to the aspirant colleges when they first apply to include their colleges to get the government portion of the salary through MPO and that result has to be maintained within the next five years period. The provision of clause 6 does not reserve any consequence of failure to keep the prescribed result and, as such, the same cannot taken as a ground for stopping or canceling the MPO of a college who failed to keep the prescribed result. Moreover the respondent did not rely upon the provision of article 6 of the নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ and since the provision of article 15 of the said নীতিমালা ১৯৯৫ does not provide for stopping or canceling the MPOs of the petitioners, this court is in irresistible view that the impugned order to stop the payment of salary of the petitioners through MPO under the impugned Memo has been made without lawful authority. In that respect this court finds merit in this rule. 

 23. It appears that after achieving the independence from the Government of British India on 14th August 1947 through the Indian Independence Act, 1947 creating two separate Dominions of India and Pakistan, the then province of Bengal was also divided into two provinces one being East Bengal, forming the eastern part of Pakistan and the other being the west Bengal forming the Dominion of India. Thereafter in order to make immediate provision for the supervision, control and development of Education and the efficient functionary of the existing educational institutions, located in East Bengal, the governor of East Bengal on 12-9-1947 at the time when the provincial legislature was not constituted, promulgate East Bengal Education Ordinance, 1947 (Ordinance No.1 of 1947) pursuant to the power vested in him under section 8(2) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 read with section 88(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935 and the Pakistan (Provisional Constitution) Order, 1947. Through the provision of section 4 of the said Ordinance the University of Dhaka (Dacca) without any prejudice to its original character as teaching and residential university, have been given the sole Power and authority to recognize and affiliate all educational institutions in East Bengal, imparting instructions and preparing students for the degree diploma, and certificate examination from after the Matriculation, High School or High Madrasha standard, that is intermediate Arts, Science and Technology; Bachelor's (pass and honours), Masters and Research Degrees, Diplomas or certificates in the subjects comprised in the faculties of Arts, Oriental Studies Islamic Study and Culture, Ancient and modem language, Architecture and Archeology, Law, Science, Medicine, Engineering Veterinary, Pisiculture, Mineralogy Journalism and other general, technical and vocational subjects. In the same statute, through the provision of section 7, the then existing Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka (Dacca) was dissolved and a new Board under the name and style East Bengal Secondary Education Board was Constituted for the purpose of control, supervision and development of Education and the efficient functioning of the educational institutions, located in East Bengal imparting instructions and preparing students for the Matriculation examination of the Calcutta University and the High School and High Madrasha examination of the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka (Dacca) or any other equivalent examination and the said newly constituted Board was given the power and authorities to recognise the said educational institutions. This Ordinance 1 of 1947 was later amended by the promulgation of the East Bengal Educational (Amendment) Ordinance 1949, effected from 7th March 1949, and through the said amendment the Madrasha education was separated from the East Bengal Secondary Education Board. This arrangement continued till 1994 when the then provincial government of East Bengal Promulgated "The East Bengal Educational Ordinance Continuance Act, 1954 upon the expiry of the Ordinance No.1 of 1947 and the said Continuance Act of 1954 was substituted by new promulgation of The East Bengal Secondary Education Act, 1955 (Act No. IV of 1955) which although named as 'Act' but actually the same was promulgated by the then Governor of East Bengal under the authority of a Proclamation dated 29th May 1954, issue by the Governor General of Pakistan under section 92A of the Government of India Act, 1935 assuming on behalf of the Governor-General, all powers vested in or exercisable by the provincial legislature under the Government of India Act, 1935. By the operation of the said Act a new Educational Board under the name and style "East Pakistan Secondary Education Board" was established, which was entrusted with the function, inter-alia, to regulate, control, and develop Secondary Education in East Bengal. This Act was operative in the then East Pakistan when the Government repealed the said Act IV of 1955 on 17 September 1961 and promulgated "The East Pakistan Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 (Ordinance No. XXXIII of 1961) to reorganize the Intermediate and Secondary Education in the East Pakistan and constituted a new Board named "Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, East Pakistan which was entrusted with the power of regulation, supervision, control and development of Intermediate and Secondary Education in the then East Pakistan. This Ordinance was further amended though the promulgation of "The East Pakistan Intermediate and Secondary Education (Amendment) Ordinance, 1962 (Ordinance No. XVI of 1962) and the original East Pakistan Board was named as Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka (Dacca) with power to the Government to establish further educational Board elsewhere in East Pakistan. In the year 1977 the then President Ziaur Rahman though Ordinance No. XVII of 1977 amended the said 1961 Act in minor fields and since then no new Act was promulgated in the filed and, as such, the 1961 Act i.e. the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education Ordinance, 1961 (Ordinance No. XXXIII of 1961) is the prevailing regulating law in the filed of Intermediate and Secondary Education in Bangladesh. 

 25. It appears that under Article 15(a) of the Constitute the Government of Bangladesh is responsible to attain through planned economic growth, a constant increase of productive forces and steady improvement in the material and cultural standard of living of the people with a view to securing to its citizen the provision of the basic necessities of life including, inter-alia, education. Further, under Article 17(a) of the Constitution the State is also responsible for adopting effective measures for the purpose of— 

 26. The Government of Bangladesh under such fundamental principle of state Policy is liable to discharge its function under the provision of law. The Ministry of Education under such constitutional mandate is only responsible to formulate policy and to act under the authority of statutory provision. 

 28. From 1992 a Division was created under Minister of Education regarding Primary and Mass Education which is being administrated by one Secretary, 2 of Joint Secretaries, some of Deputy Secretaries and Assistant Secretaries. But despite such Administrative setup and sincere intent of the Government to develop the educational Sector of Bangladesh, it did not pay any heed to several recommendations of Education Commission formed at different times namely (i) Dr Kudrat-e-Khuda Commission of 1974, (ii) The Interim Education report of 1979 (iii) The Education Commission 1988 known as Mofiz Commission. Although their recommendations were not accepted by the Government of the day, yet the Government from time to time relied upon some portions of these recommendations and implemented those by way of statutory rules and order (SRO) i.e. Circular know in vernacular as পরিপত্র. 

 29. It appears that there prevails no comprehensive law in respect of Administration of Secondary and Intermediate Education including Primary and Mass Education in Bangladesh, excepting that of Act XXXIII of 1961 and the law relating to creation of other three Secondary Education Boards. Although the Government has formulated workable instruments to administer the Secondary and Intermediate Education including the Primary and Mass Education by পরিপত্র, yet such an arrangement may be workable for temporary period. To make sound provision for administration in the Education sector, as aforesaid, the Government is required to obtain a comprehensive law from the legislature and as the time is rife, this court is constrained to observe that unless such comprehensive law is promulgated, the allegation of corruption, on the highest degree prevailing in tire Education Sector cannot be wiped out. The state of affairs must be taken into consideration by the New Government of Sheikh Hasina who has come to the power with the mandate of the People for change.
